text:
Sampled HR@10 measures competition within the sampled candidate set; it does not reliably estimate full-catalog HR@10. Model rankings can reverse even in expectation, so repeated sampling reduces sampling uncertainty without eliminating systematic bias. Foundational [Krichene–Rendle research](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) establishes this distinction; [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and recovery of model rankings.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: construct fixed prefix–next-item probes exclusively from training histories, excluding each target from its input. For each probe, measure full-catalog target rank, number of eligible items outscoring the target, and target score minus the tenth-highest eligible competitor score. Report ranks around the top-10 boundary and repeat candidate sampling with fixed, shared seeds across compared checkpoints. Summarize per-user hit probabilities and rank variation; use paired user-level bootstrap intervals for differences, keeping candidate-sampling variability separate from between-user uncertainty. These are proposed audits, not established guarantees or replacements for the benchmark.

Stratify results by target popularity computed from training interactions, history length and users’ historical popularity exposure; report stratum sizes and uncertainty. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds random negative sampling can reinforce popularity bias and favor head items. [2024 reproduction research](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/33989/) also finds popularity-bias conclusions depend on user grouping and evaluation strategy. Apply these supplementary measurements to each single GRU4Rec category model; preserve the pinned evaluator and select using the unchanged four-category macro validation HR@10.
